key_facts: **Polymorphic light eruption (PLE)** is the commonest photodermatosis: itchy papules, vesicles or plaques hours to days after the first strong sun of spring or a holiday.
Affects exposed skin that is usually covered in winter (V of neck, arms), sparing the face often; settles over days without sun.
Tends to improve over the summer ('hardening').
Prevention: sun protection, gradual exposure; potent topical steroid for 5–7 days for flares.
Refer if severe for prophylactic phototherapy (hardening); exclude lupus (check ANA/Ro if suspicious).

sections.title: Overview
blocks: The commonest **idiopathic (primary) photodermatosis**: a recurrent, itchy, non-scarring eruption on sun-exposed skin appearing hours to a couple of days after the first significant sun exposure of spring/summer or of a sunny holiday. Also called polymorphous light eruption or "prickly heat"/"sun allergy" by the public (not true prickly heat — that is miliaria). Affects roughly 10–20% of people in northern Europe; more common in women, onset usually in the teens to 30s; all skin types.

sub: Up to 1 in 5 people in northern Europe; women more; onset in the teens to 30s.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: A delayed-type (cell-mediated) immune reaction to a UV-induced skin antigen. Normally UV exposure suppresses skin immunity; in PMLE that **UV-induced immunosuppression fails**, so the newly photo-induced antigen provokes inflammation. **UVA is the main trigger in most patients** (UVB alone in a minority, both in some) — which is why a high-SPF but weak-UVA sunscreen fails (Case 1). Skin "hardens" with repeated exposure, so it is typically worse early in the season and improves through summer. Family history in a proportion.

ul: Delayed-type hypersensitivity to a UV-induced skin antigen, with failure of normal UV immunosuppression.
Mainly UVA; can occur through window glass.
**"It's an allergy to sunscreen"**: PLE is a reaction to light itself, although sunscreen allergy can occur.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Normally UV **dampens skin immunity**; in PLE this fails and the immune system attacks UV-altered skin.

mech.t: UV (mainly UVA) alters skin proteins, creating new antigens.
Normal UV-induced immunosuppression (Langerhans cell migration, regulatory T cells) does not occur.
T cells react hours to days later, producing itchy papules and vesicles.
Repeated gradual exposure restores tolerance, so PLE eases as summer goes on.

histo: Papillary dermal oedema with a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate; spongiosis. Biopsy if lupus is suspected.

ul: **Itch or burning** often starting within hours (Case 1: 30 minutes); rash within hours to 1–3 days.
Morphology varies between patients but is **usually consistent in one individual**: small papules (commonest), papulovesicles, plaques, targetoid/EM-like lesions, rarely purpuric.
Sites: **V of neck, upper chest, outer arms/forearms, dorsal hands, legs**; face often relatively spared (habitually exposed, hardened).
Resolves over days–2 weeks without scarring **if further sun is avoided**; can spread and persist with continued exposure (Case 1 extension to trunk).
Variant: **juvenile spring eruption** (papulovesicles on helices of ears in boys).

sub: Pinpoint papular variant common; may look skin-coloured or hypopigmented.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical: timing (first strong sun), photodistribution, recurrent seasonal pattern, normal health. In **severe, atypical or treatment-resistant** cases specialists consider: **ANA, anti-Ro/La antibodies** (exclude lupus — SCLE can be triggered by sun and by drugs), **porphyrin screen** (exclude erythropoietic protoporphyria/other porphyrias), skin biopsy (dermal oedema, perivascular lymphocytes — non-specific but helps exclude lupus), and **phototesting/provocation testing** in a photobiology unit. Always take a full drug history to exclude drug-induced photosensitivity.

ddx.name: Sunburn
ddx.f: Uniform painful erythema; no papules; dose-related; within hours, peaks 24 h

ddx.name: Drug-induced photosensitivity
ddx.f: New photosensitiser (doxycycline, thiazide, NSAID…); "exaggerated sunburn" or eczema; ask about drugs

ddx.name: Cutaneous lupus (SCLE/DLE)
ddx.f: Persistent annular/psoriasiform or scarring plaques; ANA/Ro positive; lasts weeks–months

ddx.name: Solar urticaria
ddx.f: Wheals within **minutes** of exposure, fade within hours

ddx.name: Actinic prurigo
ddx.f: Childhood onset, excoriated papules/nodules incl. covered sites, cheilitis, persists into winter

ddx.name: Erythema multiforme
ddx.f: Targets on palms/soles; HSV/drug trigger; not photodistributed

ddx.name: Airborne contact dermatitis / CAD
ddx.f: Eczematous, chronic; shaded sites involved (airborne) or older man, lichenified (CAD)

sections.title: Management

ul: Avoid further sun until settled; cool showers/compresses, emollient.
**Oral non-sedating antihistamine** for itch (helps itch, not the rash) — hydroxyzine in Case 1 had limited effect.
OTC hydrocortisone 1% is usually too weak for established PMLE on limbs/trunk.

**Short course (5–7 days, up to ~2 weeks) of a potent topical corticosteroid** (e.g. betamethasone valerate 0.1%, mometasone 0.1%) to the trunk/limbs; avoid potent on face — use moderate for ≤5–7 days if needed.

Severe extensive flares: a **short course of oral prednisolone** may be used (GP/specialist decision; e.g. a few days at the start of a holiday is a recognised specialist strategy for predictable attacks).
Graded, gradual sun exposure in spring ("natural hardening").
**Broad-spectrum SPF 30–50+ with high UVA protection (UK 4–5 star UVA or EU "UVA" circle logo)**, applied generously 15–30 min before going out and re-applied every 2 h and after swimming.
Clothing, hat, shade, avoid 11:00–15:00; UVA passes through glass (car side windows, conservatory).
Severe recurrent: **referral for prophylactic phototherapy ("hardening") with narrowband UVB or PUVA in spring**; hydroxychloroquine or immunosuppressants are rarely used (specialist).

blocks: **SPF is not the only measure of sunscreen quality** — choose by UVA protection too.

head: Parameter
What to advise
rows: **SPF (UVB/sunburn protection)**
SPF **30 minimum; SPF 50+** for photodermatoses
**UVA protection**
**UK star rating 4–5 stars** (Boots scale) or **EU "UVA" circle logo** (UVA-PF ≥ ⅓ of SPF). Critical — UVA drives PMLE (~75% UVA-induced), drug phototoxicity, phytophotodermatitis, CAD
**Visible light** (PCT, some CAD/solar urticaria)
Chemical filters inadequate — **mineral (titanium dioxide/zinc oxide) tinted/iron-oxide sunscreens**; Dundee cream via specialists
**Broad spectrum / photostable**
Look for "broad spectrum"; photostable filters
**Water resistance**
Water-resistant if swimming/sweating, but **re-apply after towelling**
**Formulation/skin type**
Fragrance-free and minimal-filter for CAD / photoallergy (avoid benzophenone/oxybenzone, octocrylene if allergic — especially with topical ketoprofen history); sprays/gels for hairy skin
**Amount**
~**2 mg/cm²** — about **6 teaspoons (~35 ml)** for an adult whole body; most people apply a third to half of this
**Timing**
Apply 15–30 min before going out; **re-apply every 2 hours** and after swimming/sweating
**Shade/timing**
Avoid **11:00–15:00** in UK summer (sun strongest); UV index ≥3 needs protection; cloud doesn't block UVA
**Glass**
**UVA passes through window glass** — car side windows, conservatories, office windows; UV-filter window film helps (PCT, CAD, drug photosensitivity)
**Clothing**
Tightly woven/UPF 50+ clothing, long sleeves, collars, **wide-brimmed hat**, UV-protective sunglasses, gloves for driving (PCT/CAD)
**Sunbeds**
**Avoid entirely** (UVA-rich; pseudoporphyria; skin cancer)
**Vitamin D**
Strict photoprotection → **10 micrograms (400 units) colecalciferol daily** (UK advice), or check levels
**Expiry/storage**
Check expiry (usually 12 months after opening); store cool
**Prescribing**
Sunscreens are **ACBS-approved** on FP10 for *genetic disorders/photodermatoses* (e.g. PMLE, PCT, CAD, porphyrias) — endorse "ACBS"; otherwise self-care purchase

ladder.t: Avoid further sun until settled; cool showers/compresses, emollient. **Oral non-sedating antihistamine** for itch (helps itch, not the rash) — hydroxyzine in Case 1 had limited effect.

**Short course (5–7 days, up to ~2 weeks) of a potent topical corticosteroid** (e.g. betamethasone valerate 0.1%, mometasone 0.1%) to the trunk/limbs; avoid potent on face — use moderate for ≤5–7 days if needed. Severe extensive flares: a **short course of oral prednisolone** may be used (GP/specialist decision; e.g. a few days at the start of a holiday is a recognised specialist strategy for predictable attacks).

Diagnostic doubt (rule out lupus/porphyria), scarring, persistent >2–3 weeks without sun, systemic features, failure of potent topical steroid, severe recurrent PMLE affecting quality of life (phototherapy referral).

ul: Distress and holiday disruption; rare link with later lupus or autoimmune thyroid disease.
Recurs each spring for years; often improves with age.

pearls: "It's not an allergy to the sun cream — it's a reaction to UVA the cream didn't block." Check the **UVA rating**, not just SPF.
Expect recurrence each spring/holiday but often milder later in summer; tends to improve over years.
Vitamin D: if strict sun avoidance, advise 10 micrograms (400 units) daily supplement (UK public health advice).
Always run a quick drug check — a new doxycycline or thiazide changes the diagnosis.

quiz.q: When should you think of Polymorphic light eruption?
quiz.a: An itchy rash on the V of the neck, forearms and backs of hands hours to a day after early-season sun, settling within days without further exposure.
A delayed immune reaction to a UV-induced skin antigen, with a failure of normal UV immunosuppression; it improves through the summer (‘hardening’).

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Broad-spectrum high-UVA sunscreen, clothing and gradual exposure; potent topical steroid for flares; refer for phototesting or hardening if severe.
Lupus (persistent rash, systemic symptoms, positive ANA) and drug photosensitivity.
